text: I’ll model each straight bevel gear as a loft between geometrically similar involute profiles whose scale converges toward the common pitch-cone apex. The two pitch cones use the exact tooth-count ratio and intersecting axes; backlash is allocated equally by thinning each member by 0.15 mm at its pitch circle. Because face width, shaft diameter, and placement were not specified, I will initially assume a 15 mm face width, 16 mm pinion shaft, 20 mm wheel shaft, and center the common apex in the cavity. I’ll first confirm the available CAD operations before building the coarse solids.

The gear axes will be +X (pinion) and +Z (wheel), with their pitch-cone apex at the cavity center. Each shaft starts at its gear’s inner face and runs outward through only the corresponding positive-side wall, avoiding an artificial shaft intersection at the apex. I’ll now build the coarse CAD and print the pitch geometry and tooth-thickness/backlash measurements.

The initial half-pitch phase leaves a small 2.83 mm³ tooth overlap, so it is not an acceptable meshing position despite the intended backlash. I’ll search one wheel-tooth period for a phase with zero solid interference, keeping the tooth geometry and specified backlash unchanged.

The coarse phase grid skipped the original 6° setting and therefore did not improve it. I’ll refine only around that contact position to quantify whether the residual is a tessellation/contact artifact or true interference.
The symmetric minimum is real rather than a missed phase. I’ll locate the tiny overlap before deciding whether it comes from tooth tips or the assumed shaft/hub geometry.

The overlap lies between tooth regions near the large ends, not in the shaft assumptions. It is 2.83 mm³ (about 0.0035% of the combined solids) and results from lofting planar involute profiles rather than generating exact spherical involutes. I will keep this documented approximation for the coarse model, inspect the full placement visually, and only then form the oil volume.

The preview confirms the assumed placement and that both shafts reach distinct positive-side walls. I’ll now subtract the combined rotating solids from the cavity, check that the result is one solid, and inspect its face types so the cavity, gear, and cylindrical shaft-bore surfaces can be tagged from actual resulting faces rather than bounding-box locations.

The oil volume is a valid single solid (2.60718 L), as requested. Its only cylindrical faces are the two shaft bores; the remaining rotor boundary consists of planar end faces and B-spline tooth/flank faces. I’ll establish patch membership by coincidence with the source faces used in the booleans, using cylinder radius only to distinguish the two explicitly assumed shafts.

A whole-face minimum is not a coincidence test because touching at one edge returns zero. I’ll instead sample interior parametric points on each resulting face; that distinguishes whether the face interior lies on the cavity, pinion, wheel, or shaft source.

The interior-point test cleanly separates all representative faces. I’ll now assign every actual fluid face to exactly one of five patches, print face counts and areas, and use the required single-call exporter so all STL seams share identical tessellation.
The unified tessellation/export is still running; I’ll wait for that same operation to finish rather than queue another cell.

The exported union is watertight and consistently wound: 3,832 triangles, zero open/non-manifold/flipped edges, and the requested 0.160 × 0.140 × 0.120 m extent. I’ll use a slightly oversized coarse Cartesian background mesh and snappyHexMesh with a fluid-side location near a cavity corner; local level-2 refinement will resolve gear and bore surfaces while the cavity walls remain coarse.
The meshing dictionaries are ready. I’ll now generate the coarse background mesh and run snappyHexMesh in-place, capturing the mesher’s final patch and cell counts.

The background mesh succeeded; snappyHexMesh stopped before meshing because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for this utility. I’ll add those mandatory files and rerun only snappyHexMesh.

The second startup check found that the local `#include "meshQualityDict"` was unresolved. I’ll ask the installed OpenFOAM distribution for its standard mesh-quality dictionary path, copy it into the case, and then rerun.
I’ll repeat that lookup with its own explicit import so the retained build script remains independently runnable.
I’ll now create all three required support dictionaries in one successful step and run snappyHexMesh.

The standard quality dictionary contains the geometric limits but not the motion-solver coefficient `errorReduction` expected by this snappy configuration. I’ll inspect the installed templates for the matching syntax before patching the case dictionary.
I’ll add the documented smoothing reduction coefficient directly after the included limits, recreate the required support files for the final script, and rerun snappyHexMesh.

That abort occurred during refinement after earlier failed runs had already altered `constant/polyMesh`; it was not starting from the pristine block mesh. I’ll make the support-file edit idempotent, regenerate the background mesh from scratch, and then run snappy once from that clean state.

OpenFOAM next requested the paired smoothing iteration count. I’ll inspect its shipped snappy dictionaries and generation-quality include to match this version exactly rather than discovering entries one by one.
The correct OpenFOAM 2512 include is `etc/caseDicts/mesh/generation/meshQualityDict.cfg`, which contains both coefficients. I’ll use that file, regenerate the pristine block mesh, and rerun snappy.

The coarse snapped mesh completed with 31,786 cells and no final snappy quality errors. I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect the boundary table to confirm that only the five requested patches remain.

The mesh has the correct single region and exactly five patches, but bare `checkMesh` fails on four faces with skewness 5.66. Snappy’s shipped boundary limit is 20 whereas bare `checkMesh` applies a stricter practical threshold here. I’ll lower snappy’s boundary-skew limit to 4, rebuild from the clean background, and let its quality rollback repair those faces.
The rebuilt mesh now satisfies snappy’s stricter boundary-skew limit. I’ll rerun the binding bare `checkMesh` and record final metrics.

Before declaring completion, I’ll consolidate the successful OpenFOAM support-file edits and meshing commands into one self-contained, idempotent final build step. This ensures the retained `build.py` reproduces the passing mesh from an empty case rather than depending on files left by earlier failed attempts.
